opus-5.5.text:
Experiments are really how you find out which of your ideas actually matter, because the field is full of plausible stories about what should help, and most of them turn out not to.

The biggest thing is ablations. Once you have a system that works reasonably well, you take pieces out one at a time and see how much the accuracy drops. That's often more informative than adding things, because it tells you what the network is actually relying on rather than what you *think* it's relying on. Sometimes a component you were very attached to barely matters, and something you added almost as an afterthought turns out to be load-bearing. You have to be willing to let the data overrule your intuition.

The second thing is looking at the failures, not just the aggregate metrics. A single number like average accuracy on a benchmark hides a lot. If you look at the actual predicted structures where the model does badly, you start to see patterns. Maybe it gets the local secondary structure right but can't assemble the global fold. Maybe it does poorly when there's little evolutionary information in the alignment. Each of those failure modes points to something different the architecture might be missing: better long-range communication, better use of the alignment, a better way to reason about geometry.

The third is fast iteration. You can't develop intuition if every experiment takes weeks. So a lot of the engineering effort goes into having smaller-scale setups that are predictive of what will happen at full scale. Then you can run many experiments, build up a feel for which kinds of changes move the needle, and save the expensive runs for ideas you already have evidence for.

Finally, I'd say it's important to bake in the right inductive biases, but to test them rather than assume them. Proteins have a lot of physical and geometric structure, and it's tempting to hard-code all of it. Some of that really helps the network, and some of it just constrains it. The experiments tell you where that line is. Over time you build up a sense that the architecture should make it easy for information to flow in the ways the problem requires, for example between the sequence alignment and the pairwise representation of residues, and then let learning do the rest.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that for us, experiments were never really about confirming a hypothesis. They were about generating the hypotheses in the first place. We had very little theory to go on about what a network "should" look like for proteins, so the loop was: build something, train it, and then stare very hard at what it got wrong.

And I mean that quite literally. We'd look at individual proteins. Which domains were well-folded, where the chain went off into nonsense, whether a beta sheet was pairing the right strands but with the wrong register. Those failure modes tell you something about what information the model can and can't move around. If the local geometry is good but the global arrangement is wrong, that's a very different problem from if the secondary structure itself is broken. The aggregate metric, the GDT or the lDDT, tells you that you're doing badly. The individual structures tell you how you're doing badly, and that's where the intuition comes from.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that we ran a lot of small, cheap experiments rather than a few big ones. You want to be able to change one thing and see the response within hours, not weeks. That's how you build up a feel for the system. You start to learn, for instance, that the network desperately wants to reason about pairs of residues rather than single residues, or that it needs some way to talk about geometry directly rather than being asked to infer it from a distance matrix. None of that was obvious a priori. It came from trying things, noticing what helped a surprising amount, and then asking why.

And I'd say the "why" step is the one people skip. When something works better than you expected, that's the most valuable moment, because it means your mental model was wrong. We tried to take those seriously. We'd go back and ask what the architecture change actually let the network do that it couldn't before, and often that would suggest the next three experiments. Ablations were part of it too, but less as a way to produce a tidy table for the paper and more as a way to find out which pieces were load-bearing. Sometimes you remove something and nothing happens, and that's informative. Sometimes you remove something and the whole thing collapses, and you learn that you'd accidentally built in something essential without understanding it.

So I suppose the short version is: we treated the model as an object of study, almost in the way an experimental biologist treats a cell. You poke it, you watch how it responds, and over time you develop a picture of what it needs, which is really a picture of what the problem itself needs.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make your intuition answer a question you can actually test. You might think, “The network needs a better way to reason about geometry.” Well, what does that mean? What change would you make, and what would you expect to improve if that explanation were right?

Then you run the experiment, and often the interesting part is where your expectation breaks. Perhaps the average accuracy improves, but the particular failures you were trying to fix are still there. That tells you that the change was useful, but your explanation of why it would be useful was incomplete.

Ablations help as well. You can build quite an elaborate story about why a component is essential, and then remove it and discover that the network does almost as well. Or you remove something that seemed fairly innocuous and performance collapses. Those are opportunities to update your understanding.

There's a complication, though: you're testing a learned system. If an architectural idea fails, it might be the wrong idea, or it might be difficult to optimize, or it might need other parts of the system to change with it. So a single result rarely settles the conceptual question.

For me, intuition comes from going around that loop repeatedly: make a prediction, run a reasonably controlled experiment, look closely at the errors, and revise the prediction. Eventually you develop a sense of which kinds of information the network can use easily and which kinds you need to make more accessible to it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make your intuition answerable to experiments. You have an idea about what the network needs to do—perhaps it needs to reason about relationships between residues—and you build something that lets you test that idea. But whether it improves the final prediction is only part of what you want to learn. Where does it improve? What kinds of mistakes remain? Did it actually use the information you thought it would use?

Ablations are useful here, although you have to be careful. If you remove a component and performance drops, that tells you the trained system depends on it. It doesn’t necessarily tell you that every successful architecture needs that component. There might be another way to learn the same computation.

So it’s a loop: you look at failures, form a hypothesis about the computation that’s missing, and design an experiment that could prove you wrong. Over time, you get a better feel for which things you should build into the architecture and which things the network can learn for itself. The intuition is really the accumulated result of those experiments.
